screens.title: Incident Response and Digital Forensics
screens.narratorSegment: Incidents will happen even with strong defenses. What separates organizations that recover quickly from those that suffer long-term harm is a disciplined incident response program and careful forensic practice. In this lesson you will learn why a written, tested incident response plan matters, how the six-phase lifecycle guides action from preparation through lessons learned, and why digital forensics must preserve evidence integrity for legal and remediation purposes. You will see concrete examples: how a runbook turns chaos into repeatable steps, how hashing proves evidence hasn’t been altered, and how an effective response team coordinates technical work with legal and communications. As you move through the screens, we’ll examine each lifecycle phase with practical tasks, common mistakes to avoid, and forensic techniques such as disk imaging and memory analysis. By the end you'll be able to explain the lifecycle, name core team roles, and describe the principles that make digital evidence admissible. Keep an eye out for the chain of custody example — it shows how careful documentation protects both the investigation and the organization.

screens.title: What is Incident Response?
screens.narratorSegment: Incident response is a structured approach for managing the aftermath of a security breach or cyberattack with three practical goals: limit impact, restore normal operations, and learn to prevent recurrence. The definition includes both technical actions — isolating systems, collecting evidence — and organizational actions — coordinating communications, engaging legal counsel, and updating policies. A concrete example: when a web server is compromised, an effective response uses a runbook to quickly isolate the host, preserve volatile data, and notify stakeholders while preserving evidence for later analysis. A common misconception is that incident response is purely technical; in reality, poor coordination with communications or legal can increase regulatory and reputational harm even if the technical team removes the attacker. Another mistake is to treat response as ad hoc; waiting until an incident occurs to assemble a team leads to chaotic decision-making. The key takeaway is that incident response combines policy, people, processes, and tools. Practice drafting a one-page runbook for a simple incident type — that exercise forces you to specify who does what, what evidence to preserve, and how to communicate, which is the foundation of reliable response.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.7 › What is Incident Response?
Core Concept

Incident Response defined

A coordinated set of actions and roles to minimize damage, collect evidence, and return services to safe operation.

Why it matters

Fast, repeatable response prevents larger outages and reduces legal and reputational exposure.

Common misconception

It's not just technical work; communications and legal are part of a successful response.

Key Takeaway

Treat incident response as an organizational capability: policy, people, and tools working together.

Analogy & Example

Think of response like emergency triage: quickly stabilize critical systems, collect evidence like vital signs, and then plan definitive treatment. Example: a compromised web server is isolated, RAM is captured, disk images are taken, and stakeholders are briefed per a runbook.

Check your understanding
  • Can you name the immediate goal of incident response?
  • What non-technical roles are essential during a breach?
  • Why should you avoid working directly on original evidence?

screens.title: IR Lifecycle Overview
screens.narratorSegment: The incident response lifecycle gives structure to actions taken before, during, and after an incident. The six commonly accepted phases are preparation, detection and analysis, containment, eradication, recovery, and post-incident activity. Preparation builds the plan, team, tools, runbooks, and logging needed to respond reliably. Detection and analysis use monitoring, alerts, and triage to confirm incidents and determine scope. Containment limits spread through isolation and access controls. Eradication removes root causes such as malware and patched vulnerabilities or rebuilt systems. Recovery safely restores services, often in phases starting with the most critical systems. Post-incident activity, or lessons learned, documents the event, updates procedures, and trains staff. A common error is treating these phases as strictly linear: in practice teams may iterate between containment and analysis as new artifacts appear. Use the lifecycle as a guide for who does what and when, and keep documentation at every phase so actions are auditable and repeatable. IR Lifecycle Overview means follow the six phases as a flexible guide; document actions at each phase to enable repeatable, auditable response.. In practical terms, the six phases that guide every response. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.7 › IR Lifecycle Overview
Process Flow

Six phases

Use these phases as a roadmap during incidents, but expect iteration and concurrent activities.

Preparation
Runbooks, tools, training, logging, backups.
Detection & Analysis
Monitoring, alerts, triage to confirm incidents.
Containment
Isolate affected systems and stop spread.
Process cards
Eradication
Remove malware, patch vulnerabilities, rebuild compromised systems.
Recovery
Validate systems are clean, restore from trusted backups, bring services back in phases.
Post-Incident
Document findings, update runbooks, and train teams based on lessons learned.
Misconception

The lifecycle is not strictly linear; detection and containment often feed each other and require iteration.

screens.title: Preparation: Policies, Tools, and Runbooks
screens.narratorSegment: Preparation is the most important phase because it determines how smoothly your team can respond under pressure. Preparation includes establishing written policies and an incident response plan, forming and training the team, acquiring forensic-capable tools, and ensuring comprehensive logging and backups. It also requires runbooks for common incidents so analysts can follow repeatable steps without inventing procedures mid-incident. For example, a web-server compromise runbook should list evidence to collect, commands to capture volatile data, the imaging workflow, who to notify, and safe recovery steps. A common mistake is deferring preparation until after an incident; that results in ad hoc decisions and missed evidence. Another trap is neglecting tabletop exercises — without practice, even a documented plan will fail in practice. Preparation also includes defining secure communication channels, legal contacts, and storage for original media. The practical outcome of preparation is speed and confidence: when an alert triggers, trained staff follow tested steps, preserving evidence and limiting harm. Preparation: Policies, Tools, and Runbooks means policies, trained teams, runbooks, logging, and tooling enable quick, consistent, and forensically sound responses.. In practical terms, build the capability before an incident occurs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.7 › Preparation
Preparation

Build capability

Define policies, train the team, procure tools, and create runbooks so responses are repeatable and defensible.

Runbooks
Step-by-step actions for common incidents to avoid ad hoc decisions.
Tools & Workflows
Forensic workstations, write blockers, logging, and secure communications.
Example Runbook excerpt
  • Verify alert authenticity and assign incident ID.
  • Preserve volatile data: capture memory image before reboot.
  • Image disks with write blocker and verify hashes.
  • Isolate host from network and notify stakeholders.
Common mistake

Waiting to procure tools and test runbooks until after an incident results in slower containment and lost evidence.

screens.title: Detecting Incidents and Performing Analysis
screens.narratorSegment: Detection and analysis turn monitoring data into confirmed incidents and a clear understanding of scope. Detection sources include SIEM alerts, IDS/IPS, endpoint protection, and user reports. Analysis means triage: confirm whether an alert represents a true incident, identify affected assets, assess severity, and determine attack type such as malware, unauthorized access, or data exfiltration. A concrete example: a spike in outbound traffic plus corrupted web application logs may indicate data exfiltration. Analysts gather logs, endpoint artifacts, and network captures to reconstruct the timeline. Prioritization is essential—triage high-impact systems first to reduce business risk. A common misconception is treating every alert as an incident; instead, apply triage rules to filter false positives and escalate confirmed incidents. Document initial findings, assign incident IDs, and preserve evidence early. Accurate detection and analysis set the stage for effective containment and inform which containment strategy will be safest and least disruptive. Detecting Incidents and Performing Analysis means use monitoring, triage, and prioritized analysis to confirm incidents, scope impact, and guide containment choices.. In practical terms, from alerts to confirmed incidents and prioritized triage. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.7 › Detection & Analysis
Detection & Analysis

Turn alerts into answers

Confirm incidents, determine scope, and prioritize response using logs, endpoint data, and network captures.

Sources
SIEM, IDS, endpoint protection, logs, and user reports.
Triage actions
Validate alerts, assign severity, preserve evidence, and document findings.
Concrete example

A SIEM alert for unusual outbound connections triggers log review. Analysts confirm a database backup file was exfiltrated via an unusual destination IP, capture packet data, and mark systems for containment. Documentation starts immediately so subsequent containment steps do not break evidence integrity.

Misconception

Not every alert is an incident. Use triage rules to avoid chasing false positives while ensuring true incidents are prioritized.

screens.title: Containment Strategies
screens.narratorSegment: Containment focuses on limiting damage and preventing further attacker activity. Containment strategies can be short-term, like isolating a server or blocking an IP address, or long-term, such as re-architecting network segments or applying compensating controls. Choosing the right containment approach requires balancing speed and preservation of evidence. For example, unplugging a host may stop lateral movement but risks losing volatile data such as R A M contents. A safer first step is to capture volatile data and then isolate the host. Another example: blocking a malicious domain at the perimeter reduces exfiltration while preserving internal systems for analysis. A common mistake is taking irreversible action without documenting context; rapid actions must be recorded with timestamps and justification. The underlying principle is to limit impact while protecting the investigative trail so eradication and recovery can proceed with confidence. Containment Strategies means containment must limit spread while preserving volatile evidence; document every action and its rationale.. In practical terms, stopping the spread while preserving evidence. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.7 › Containment
Containment

Stop the spread

Select containment actions that reduce impact while preserving the forensic trail and volatile evidence.

Short-term
Isolation, firewall blocks, disable accounts to immediately limit spread.
Long-term
Network segmentation and architectural changes to prevent recurrence.
Concrete scenario

If a server shows active data exfiltration, capture memory and network traffic, then isolate the host or block the destination. Recording each action ensures subsequent forensic analysis remains valid.

Pro tip

Prefer containment steps that are reversible where possible and document why irreversible actions were necessary.

screens.title: Eradication: Remove the Root Cause
screens.narratorSegment: Eradication means eliminating the cause of the incident so attackers cannot return. This commonly involves removing malware, patching exploited vulnerabilities, changing credentials, and addressing persistence mechanisms. In some cases you will rebuild compromised systems from trusted backups to ensure no residual tools remain. The critical part of eradication is validation: confirm that the attacker’s access vectors are closed and that no backdoors or scheduled tasks remain. A frequent mistake is to restore systems from backups without ensuring backups are clean; that risks reintroducing the same compromise. Another pitfall is incomplete remediation—fixing a single host while ignoring lateral access can allow the attacker to re-establish themselves. Use comprehensive scans, integrity checks, and re-imaging when necessary. Document eradication steps and update runbooks to prevent recurrence. The goal is not only to remove the immediate threat but to make it difficult for similar attacks to succeed in future. Eradication: Remove the Root Cause means remove attacker tools and access, validate fixes, and rebuild or patch systems so the threat cannot recur.. In practical terms, patching, cleaning, and rebuilding to eliminate attacker access. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.7 › Eradication
Eradication

Remove attacker access

Patching, malware removal, credential changes, and rebuilding compromised systems are common eradication actions.

Validation
Confirm that persistence mechanisms are removed and access vectors are closed.
When to rebuild
If integrity is uncertain, rebuild from trusted backups rather than attempting in-place cleanups.
Example

After malware removal, patch the exploited service, rotate credentials, and run integrity checks. If evidence shows attacker-created tasks, rebuild from a verified backup to ensure no hidden backdoors remain.

Misconception

Eradication is not complete until you validate that the attacker cannot return; visible cleanup is not enough without validation.

screens.title: Recovery: Restoring Services Safely
screens.narratorSegment: Recovery is the controlled return of systems and services to normal operation after eradication is complete and validated. The recovery phase should be phased: bring critical systems online first after verifying they are clean and patched, restore data from trusted backups, and test services under controlled conditions. Before restoring a critical database, for example, verify that the root cause has been eradicated and that backups used for restoration are not contaminated. Failure to verify leads to immediate re-compromise. Recovery also involves monitoring restored systems closely for evidence of recurrence. A common misconception is that recovery is purely a technical restoration; it also requires stakeholder coordination, communication plans, and sometimes regulatory notifications. Document each recovery step and preserve logs from the restored environment for post-incident analysis. The key is cautious, validated restoration to avoid bouncing back into another incident. Recovery: Restoring Services Safely means restore systems in phases after confirming eradication and verifying backup integrity to prevent re-compromise.. In practical terms, validate, restore, and bring systems back online in phases. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Forensics Techniques: Imaging, Memory, and Logs
screens.narratorSegment: Digital forensics is the process of identifying, preserving, analyzing, and presenting digital evidence in a way that supports investigations and legal proceedings. The core principles are preservation, chain of custody, and integrity. Preservation means working on copies not originals; use write blockers and capture forensic images to avoid altering original drives. Chain of custody is a documented log of who handled evidence, when, and why, ensuring admissibility. Integrity is verified with hashing: compute and record hashes before and after imaging. Common techniques include disk imaging for persistent storage, memory analysis for volatile artifacts, log analysis to reconstruct events, and network forensics for packet captures. Module 6 › Chapter 6.7 › Digital Forensics
Forensics

Preserve, verify, and analyze

Work on copies, compute hashes, maintain chain of custody, and use appropriate tools for disk, memory, and log analysis.

Disk imaging
Create bit-for-bit copies with a write blocker and record hashes for integrity verification.
Memory analysis
Capture RAM early to preserve volatile processes and network connections for analysis.
Imaging example
# BE EXTREMELY CAREFUL: dd can overwrite disks if used incorrectly
# Create a forensic image of a disk
dd if=/dev/sda of=/mnt/forensics/disk_image.dd bs=4M conv=noerror,sync status=progress
# Calculate a SHA-256 hash of the image
sha256sum /mnt/forensics/disk_image.dd
Safety notes

Always image originals using a write blocker, record original and image hashes, and work on copies only. Log all actions in the chain of custody.

Incidents will happen even with strong defenses. What separates organizations that recover quickly from those that suffer long-term harm is a disciplined incident response program and careful forensic practice. In this lesson you will learn why a written, tested incident response plan matters, how the six-phase lifecycle guides action from preparation through lessons learned, and why digital forensics must preserve evidence integrity for legal and remediation purposes. You will see concrete examples: how a runbook turns chaos into repeatable steps, how hashing proves evidence hasn’t been altered, and how an effective response team coordinates technical work with legal and communications. As you move through the screens, we’ll examine each lifecycle phase with practical tasks, common mistakes to avoid, and forensic techniques such as disk imaging and memory analysis. By the end you'll be able to explain the lifecycle, name core team roles, and describe the principles that make digital evidence admissible. Keep an eye out for the chain of custody example — it shows how careful documentation protects both the investigation and the organization.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain why a well-defined incident response plan reduces damage and supports legal and regulatory needs. You will describe the six-phase incident response lifecycle: preparation, detection and analysis, containment, eradication, recovery, and post-incident activity. You will identify common team roles and responsibilities, from an incident manager to forensic analysts and communication leads, and explain why coordination with legal and HR matters. Finally, you will understand core digital forensics principles — preservation, chain of custody, and integrity — and how common techniques such as disk imaging and memory analysis support investigations. Each objective connects to hands-on tasks: maintaining runbooks, verifying hashes, and documenting evidence movement. These are practical skills that help you make decisions under pressure and create defensible records of what was done. As you study, practice writing a runbook entry and filling the chain of custody form for a simulated image to cement these concepts.

This second objectives screen focuses on practical forensic techniques and procedural skills you must practice. You will learn to perform safe disk imaging and memory captures, using tools and guidance such as creating bit-for-bit images and verifying hashes. You will practice log and network forensics methods to reconstruct events. You will also be able to document a chain of custody correctly, including timestamps, handlers, actions, and signatures, which preserves admissibility. Finally, you will learn to create runbooks and test them so that common incidents can be managed with repeatable steps. Together these objectives build muscle memory: imaging without altering originals, verifying integrity with hashing, and capturing volatile evidence before reboot. These skills reduce the risk of contamination and help investigators answer who, what, when, and how. In exercises you will fill a chain of custody example and run a simulated imaging workflow using documented commands and verification steps.

Incident response is a structured approach for managing the aftermath of a security breach or cyberattack with three practical goals: limit impact, restore normal operations, and learn to prevent recurrence. The definition includes both technical actions — isolating systems, collecting evidence — and organizational actions — coordinating communications, engaging legal counsel, and updating policies. A concrete example: when a web server is compromised, an effective response uses a runbook to quickly isolate the host, preserve volatile data, and notify stakeholders while preserving evidence for later analysis. A common misconception is that incident response is purely technical; in reality, poor coordination with communications or legal can increase regulatory and reputational harm even if the technical team removes the attacker. Another mistake is to treat response as ad hoc; waiting until an incident occurs to assemble a team leads to chaotic decision-making. The key takeaway is that incident response combines policy, people, processes, and tools. Practice drafting a one-page runbook for a simple incident type — that exercise forces you to specify who does what, what evidence to preserve, and how to communicate, which is the foundation of reliable response.

The incident response lifecycle gives structure to actions taken before, during, and after an incident. The six commonly accepted phases are preparation, detection and analysis, containment, eradication, recovery, and post-incident activity. Preparation builds the plan, team, tools, runbooks, and logging needed to respond reliably. Detection and analysis use monitoring, alerts, and triage to confirm incidents and determine scope. Containment limits spread through isolation and access controls. Eradication removes root causes such as malware and patched vulnerabilities or rebuilt systems. Recovery safely restores services, often in phases starting with the most critical systems. Post-incident activity, or lessons learned, documents the event, updates procedures, and trains staff. A common error is treating these phases as strictly linear: in practice teams may iterate between containment and analysis as new artifacts appear. Use the lifecycle as a guide for who does what and when, and keep documentation at every phase so actions are auditable and repeatable. In practical terms, the six phases that guide every response. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Preparation is the most important phase because it determines how smoothly your team can respond under pressure. Preparation includes establishing written policies and an incident response plan, forming and training the team, acquiring forensic-capable tools, and ensuring comprehensive logging and backups. It also requires runbooks for common incidents so analysts can follow repeatable steps without inventing procedures mid-incident. For example, a web-server compromise runbook should list evidence to collect, commands to capture volatile data, the imaging workflow, who to notify, and safe recovery steps. A common mistake is deferring preparation until after an incident; that results in ad hoc decisions and missed evidence. Another trap is neglecting tabletop exercises — without practice, even a documented plan will fail in practice. Preparation also includes defining secure communication channels, legal contacts, and storage for original media. Containment strategies can be short-term, like isolating a server or blocking an IP address, or long-term, such as re-architecting network segments or applying compensating controls.
